Lord's Prayer
LORDZ PRAIR
noun phrase (biblical text)
From Old English drihten (Lord, ruler) + Old English gebed (prayer, from biddan, to ask, pray). The designation “Lord's Prayer” (Oratio Dominica in the Latin tradition) is not found in Scripture itself but has been applied since at least Tertullian (c. 200 AD) to the model prayer Jesus taught his disciples in Matthew 6:9–13 (and in a shorter form in Luke 11:1–4). It is the Lord's in a double sense: given by the Lord Jesus as a pattern for prayer, and addressed to the Lord God as Father.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Lord's Prayer is the model prayer Jesus gave his disciples when asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). Delivered within the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 6:9–13) as a corrective to hypocritical public prayer (Matt 6:5–8) and vain repetition (Matt 6:7), it is not a formula to be mechanically repeated but a pattern (“pray then in this way”) that structures the whole of Christian petition. The prayer moves from doxological address (“Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name”) through kingdom petition (“Your kingdom come, Your will be done”) to daily provision (“give us this day our daily bread”), to forgiveness and its reciprocal (“forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors”), to spiritual protection (“do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil”), and closes with a doxology (“for Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever”). The structure itself is theologically instructive: petition begins with God's name and kingdom (not with the petitioner's needs), places daily provision after doxological priority, and grounds the forgiveness of debts in the practitioner's own prior forgiveness of others (Matt 6:14–15). The Reformers reclaimed the Lord's Prayer as the Christian's divinely-given curriculum for prayer: Luther wrote on it extensively; Calvin's Institutes devoted a major section to it; the Westminster Shorter Catechism devoted Questions 98–107 to it as “a perfect rule of prayer.”

Webster 1828 Definition

The model prayer Jesus gave his disciples (Matt 6:9–13) as a pattern for Christian petition — beginning with God's name and kingdom, proceeding to daily provision and mutual forgiveness, and closing with doxological ascription; held by the Reformed tradition to be a perfect summary and curriculum of the whole discipline of prayer.

LORD'S PRAYER, n. The model prayer recorded in Matthew 6:9–13 and Luke 11:2–4, given by Christ to his disciples as the pattern (“pray then in this way”) of all Christian prayer.

2. STRUCTURE: (1) Address — Our Father who is in heaven; (2) Adoration — hallowed be Your name; (3) Kingdom petition — Your kingdom come, Your will be done; (4) Provision — give us this day our daily bread; (5) Forgiveness — forgive us our debts; (6) Reciprocal condition — as we forgive our debtors; (7) Protection — do not lead us into temptation; (8) Deliverance — but deliver us from evil; (9) Doxology — for Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory.

3. NOT A FORMULA, A PATTERN: “pray then in this way” (Matt 6:9, houtōs = thus, in this manner) indicates a model for structure and priority, not a verbal formula to be recited without understanding — the very repetition Christ just condemned (Matt 6:7) suggests liturgical recitation divorced from meaning.

4. REFORMED USE: Westminster Shorter Catechism Q&A 98–107 expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition as “a perfect rule of prayer”; Luther's Large Catechism gives it extended treatment; Calvin's Institutes III.20 uses it as the organizing structure of his theology of prayer.

5. DOXOLOGY NOTE: “For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen” (Matt 6:13b) appears in the majority of Greek manuscripts; while absent from some early Alexandrian witnesses, it was used liturgically from at least the Didache (c. 100 AD) and is included in the traditional Protestant rendering.

Key Scripture

Matt 6:9 — "Pray, then, in this way: 'Our Father who is in heaven, hallowed be Your name."

Matt 6:10 — "Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."

Matt 6:11 — "Give us this day our daily bread."

Matt 6:13 — "And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. (For Yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen.)'"

Modern Corruption

The Lord's Prayer is corrupted in two directions: liberal revision that alters its language to remove patriarchal address (“Our Father”), and evangelical neglect that treats corporate recitation as vain repetition and substitutes extemporaneous prayer without the Lord's Prayer's structured discipline.

expand to see more

Progressive denominations have revised the Lord's Prayer to remove its patriarchal address — substituting “Our Parent” or “Our Father and Mother” for “Our Father who is in heaven.” This is not a hermeneutical adjustment but a theological replacement: the address “Father” (Pater in Greek) is the specific term Jesus used for God (John 17:1; Matt 11:25–27) and the term by which the Spirit of adoption causes the regenerate to cry out to God (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). To change it is to change the God being addressed. The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed opens “I believe in God the Father almighty” — a confessional commitment that rules out gender-neutral revision of the divine address.

Evangelical neglect runs in the opposite direction: the avoidance of liturgical forms, including the Lord's Prayer, on the grounds that repeated recitation constitutes the vain repetition Christ condemned (Matt 6:7). But Christ condemned battologein — empty babble, meaningless multiplication of words — not the use of fixed, theologically loaded prayer forms. The Psalms are a divinely given fixed-form prayer and praise book used repeatedly through Israel's and the church's liturgical life. The Lord's Prayer, taught as a pattern, functions as the curriculum that shapes the Christian's whole prayer life when it is received and meditated upon, not merely recited.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Lord's Prayer's structure follows the pattern of the Jewish Kaddish and Amidah prayers (address, hallowing of the name, kingdom petition, provision, forgiveness), transposing them into a distinctly Trinitarian and covenantal register for the New Covenant community.

expand to see more

Aramaic Abba (Father) — the intimate address that Jesus used (Mark 14:36) and that the Spirit of adoption places on the lips of the regenerate (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6); “Our Father” begins the prayer in this register of covenantal intimacy

Greek epiousios — “daily” or “for today” (Matt 6:11); a uniquely difficult Greek word used almost nowhere else in the language — possibly “sufficient for the coming day,” grounding daily provision in the manna-pattern of Exod 16

Greek opheilemē / opheiletēs — debt, debtor; Matthew uses the commercial/legal term (Luke uses “sins”), emphasizing that forgiveness is a cancellation of moral obligation before God and a model for how the forgiven must treat others

Greek peirasmos — temptation, trial, testing; “do not lead us into temptation” does not suggest God tempts (Jas 1:13) but asks God not to permit testing beyond our capacity — the request for protective providence against the evil one's strategies

Didache 8:3 (c. 100 AD): the earliest post-apostolic Christian document instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily — confirming its liturgical centrality from the earliest church

Usage

"Calvin's exposition of the Lord's Prayer in Institutes III.20.34–49 identifies the petition “Your kingdom come” as the prayer for the advancement of the Gospel and the suppression of everything that opposes God's reign — a petition that encompasses personal, ecclesiastical, and civil dimensions of God's kingly rule."

"The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q&A 98–107) teaches children to pray the Lord's Prayer as a systematic curriculum: each petition expands into a set of specific requests that train the soul in the pattern of gospel-centered, kingdom-oriented, grace-dependent prayer."

"Thomas Watson's The Lord's Prayer (1692) treats the prayer as a checklist of the soul's proper orientation before God — the address tests whether we pray with filial trust, the hallowing tests whether we pray with awe, the kingdom petition tests whether we pray with evangelistic concern, and so on through every petition."
